pages.title: Replace a track with a probability map

blocks.text: Repeatedly prepare an electron in the same atomic state and measure its position. A pattern of possible outcomes emerges. Quantum mechanics describes that pattern rather than a tiny planet-like path.
An atomic orbital is a one-electron wave function for an atom. It identifies an allowed state and supports predictions of where an electron may be found.

Each position measurement records one outcome. The orbital description predicts a pattern across many identically prepared measurements, not a tiny cloud of fractions of one electron. The total probability of finding the electron somewhere is 1.

pages.transition: Give the probability map a precise mathematical meaning.

pages.title: Interpret the wave function

blocks.text: The Schrödinger equation yields allowed wave functions ψ and energies. The quantity |ψ|² is position probability density. In a small volume, the probability is approximately |ψ|² multiplied by that volume.
A drawn orbital boundary encloses a chosen large fraction of the probability. It is not a hard wall; the electron is not confined inside a solid coloured lobe.

Probability density may be large at a point while the probability for an extremely small region remains small. A larger surrounding volume can contribute more total probability even with a smaller local density. This is why a density diagram and a radial probability graph answer different questions.

pages.transition: Label the allowed states systematically, beginning with the shell.

pages.title: Let n identify the shell

blocks.text: The principal quantum number n=1, 2, 3,… identifies a shell. Larger n generally means larger orbital size. For hydrogen-like atoms, the basic energy depends on n alone.
A shell contains n² orbitals and holds at most 2n² electrons. This maximum does not mean every atom fills an entire shell before another begins; relative orbital energies also matter.

For n=4, allowed l values are 0, 1, 2, 3. The subshells therefore contain 1+3+5+7=16 orbitals, agreeing with n²=16. At most 2×16=32 electrons fit. Counting the subshells explains the formula instead of treating 2n² as an unexplained rule.

pages.transition: Within each shell, distinguish subshells and spatial states.

pages.title: Use l and mₗ to distinguish orbitals

blocks.text: For fixed n, the azimuthal quantum number l runs from 0 to n−1. Values 0, 1, 2, 3 label s, p, d, f subshells. Thus n=3 allows 3s, 3p, 3d but not 3f.
The magnetic quantum number mₗ runs from−l to+l in integer steps, producing 2l+1 orbitals: s, p, d, f contain 1, 3, 5, 7 orbitals respectively.

For a 3d subshell, n=3, l=2. Its mₗ values are−2,−1, 0,+1,+2: five orbitals. Each supports two opposite-spin electrons, giving capacity 10. The five mₗ values label states; they are not five different principal shells.

pages.transition: Add spin without confusing it with orbital direction or electric charge.

pages.title: Keep spin separate from spatial state

blocks.text: The spin quantum number mₛ has values+1/2 or−1/2. Along with n, l and mₗ, it labels an electron state in the basic atomic description.
For p, l=1 and mₗ=−1, 0,+1 give three orbitals. Each supports two spin states, giving six electrons maximum. Spin is intrinsic; it is not literally a ball rotating around its axis.

Two electrons in the same spatial orbital have the same n, l and spatial-state label. They can differ in mₛ, one+1/2 and one−1/2. Their spin labels are numbers in the state description, not positive and negative electric charges.

pages.transition: Use the labels to interpret the simplest orbital shape.

pages.title: Understand spherical s orbitals

blocks.text: An s orbital has spherical symmetry: at a fixed distance from the nucleus, probability density is independent of direction. The 1s orbital has no node; 2s has a radial node.
A node is a region where the wave function and probability density are zero. An s orbital is a probability distribution, not a spherical shell along which the electron travels.

The 1s probability density is largest at the nucleus, but the probability at an exact mathematical point is not the same quantity as density. A radial probability includes the volume of a thin spherical shell. Distinguish these statements before interpreting a textbook graph.

pages.transition: Compare spherical distributions with directional p and d shapes.

pages.title: Read p and d orbital drawings

blocks.text: The conventional pₓ, pᵧ, p_z drawings show two lobes along three perpendicular directions. Each p orbital has a nodal plane through the nucleus. Opposite signs on lobes denote wave-function phase, not opposite electric charges.
Most d orbitals have four-lobed drawings; d_z² has two lobes and a ring-like region. All five belong to l=2 despite their different shapes.

The pₓ, pᵧ, p_z pictures are convenient spatial orientations in a degenerate p subshell. Degenerate means equal energy in the isolated atom before external-field effects. Different orientations do not mean that one p orbital is intrinsically a different kind of subshell.

pages.transition: Nodes give another way to compare states with similar shapes.

pages.title: Count radial and angular nodes

blocks.text: For hydrogen-like orbitals, total nodes=n−1, angular nodes=l and radial nodes=n−l−1. A radial change and an angular change describe different features of the wave function.
For 3p, n=3 and l=1: total nodes=2, angular nodes=1, radial nodes=3−1−1=1. The angular node is a plane; the radial node is a spherical surface.

For 4d, n=4 and l=2. Total nodes=3, angular nodes=2 and radial nodes=4−2−1=1. Compare 3d: total 2, angular 2, radial 0. The same d angular pattern can coexist with a different radial distribution in another shell.

pages.transition: Test the allowed labels through explicit examples.

pages.title: Test a quantum-number set

blocks.text: Is (n, l, mₗ)=(3, 2,−2) allowed? For n=3, l may be 0, 1, 2; for l=2, mₗ may be−2,−1, 0,+1,+2. Yes: it labels a 3d orbital.
The set(2, 2, 0) fails: n=2 allows only l=0 or 1. Check n first, then l, then mₗ, rather than memorising every possible combination.

Consider(3, 1, 2,+1/2). Although n=3 and l=1 are allowed, mₗ=2 is not: a p subshell allows only−1, 0,+1. The set(3, 1, 0,+1) also fails because spin must be±1/2. Check all four restrictions independently.

Find the number of orbitals with n=3 and mₗ=0. The allowed subshells l=0, 1, 2 each contain one mₗ=0 state, so there are three such orbitals. A quantum-number restriction can select across several subshells rather than one whole shell.

pages.transition: Unify the vocabulary before using orbitals to fill many-electron atoms.

blocks.text: A shell fixes n; a subshell fixes n and l; an orbital specifies an allowed spatial state. Each orbital accommodates two opposite-spin electrons. Its wave function supplies probability predictions.

Orbit and orbital are different concepts. A probability boundary, a node and a phase all describe a quantum state; none represents a miniature electron track or a differently charged part of an electron.

questions.question: How many orbitals are in the n=3 shell?
Can 2d exist?
questions.answer: No. n=2 allows l=0 or 1, whereas d requires l=2.

questions.question: How many electrons fit a d subshell?
questions.answer: Five orbitals times two gives ten electrons.

questions.question: What do opposite signs on lobes indicate?
questions.answer: Wave-function phase, not positive and negative electric charges.

questions.question: Is an orbital boundary a physical wall?
questions.answer: No. It encloses a chosen probability fraction; the wave function extends beyond it.

questions.question: Is |ψ|² itself the probability at a point?
questions.answer: It is probability density. A region’s probability also depends on its volume.
